## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/about
About Final Finish Epoxy | Flake Floors, Edmonton

Denis · Final Finish Denis runs Final Finish in Edmonton. Final Finish Epoxy Coatings was founded by Denis. We do quality floor makeovers in Edmonton, Alberta. The floors are flake, and we use Torginol products. The person quoting your floor is the person on it. Final Finish · Edmonton How we work Denis looks at the concrete first. Every job starts the same way. A free estimate comes from photos of the floor or from a visit, and the conversation is about the slab before it is about colour. There is no showroom and no street address on this site, because the work happens at yours. Final Finish is a service-area business based in Edmonton. Where we work says the rest. The order of work Grind, fill, coat, finish. A free estimate, from your photos or an in-person visit. Grinding, to open the surface of the concrete. Cosmetic crack filling. The flake broadcast, then the scrape. The top coat, plus an Anti-Slip Coating where a room needs one. Installation usually runs two days, and it varies with the concrete. The process page goes through each step properly. What you get in writing Your quote is the written agreement. Prices, timing, and coverage terms are not published on this site. They are decisions about your floor, and they belong in the document Denis sends you. That is a deliberate choice. A number on a website that has not seen your slab is a guess, and you would end up renegotiating it anyway. See the warranty page for how that works.

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/process
How a Flake Floor Gets Built | Final Finish Edmonton

The sequence How a flake floor is installed. Six steps, in this order, for a flake floor. Installation usually runs two days, and it varies with the concrete underneath. Final Finish · Edmonton 01 A free estimate Send photos of the floor, or book a visit. Either works, and both are free. Denis wants to see the concrete, what is on it now, and any cracks you already know about. 02 Grinding The slab is ground to open the surface so the coating can bond. It is loud, dusty work, and the room has to be empty before it starts. The diamond grinding guide explains the profile it leaves. 03 Cosmetic crack filling Visible cracks are filled so they do not read through the finish. If something turns up that is structural rather than cosmetic, you hear about it then, not later. The cracks and spalling guide covers what gets assessed. 04 The flake broadcast Flake is broadcast into the coat while it is still open. This is where the colour and the pattern of the floor are set. The featured colours are on the finishes page. 05 The scrape Once it has set, the surface is scraped back. That is what turns a loose broadcast into a flat floor you can walk on and clean. 06 The top coat The last coat goes over everything. Where a room needs more grip, an Anti-Slip Coating goes on instead, and that is a decision we make with you. The slip-resistance guide covers the trade-offs. Two things this page will not tell you: when you can park on it, and what it costs.

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/cold-weather-floor-coating-edmonton/
Cold-Weather Floor Coating Tips | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / local guide local guide · Edmonton floor library Cold-Weather Floor Coating Tips Plan Edmonton cold-weather floor coating around garage temperatures, cure windows, and diamond-grind prep so winter installs stay controlled and documented. Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor An Edmonton winter does not automatically rule out a floor-coating project. It changes what must be controlled and recorded. The important conditions are not the temperature in a weather app alone; they are the temperature and moisture conditions at the slab, in the work zone, and in the stored materials throughout preparation, application, and cure. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Environment and Climate Change Canada’s Edmonton city dataset includes daily temperature normals, extremes, and counts of cold days for the 1991–2020 normal period ( Edmonton climate normals ). That official record supports a practical conclusion: a winter quote needs a cold-weather control plan, not an assumption that an attached garage or loading area will remain suitable. Think in zones, not one thermostat reading Divide the project into four temperature zones: Outside: affects open-door events, deliveries, exhaust placement, and replacement air. Material storage: affects the temperature of resin, hardener, repair products, and aggregates before mixing. Room air: affects worker comfort, ventilation, and product cure. Concrete slab: may lag far behind a short burst of warm air and can vary near doors, walls, drains, or unheated edges. Ask the contractor which temperatures the product data sheet requires, where measurements will be taken, and how frequently they will be logged. “The garage will be heated” does not answer those questions. The winter go/no-go sheet Use a small table at the pre-start meeting and again before each coat. Check Evidence to record If it is outside the product limit Ambient air Time, location, calibrated reading Pause or correct enclosure/heating Slab surface Several readings, especially at edges and door Continue conditioning; do not average away a cold spot Relative humidity Reading in the work zone Follow product limit and condensation controls Dew-point margin Air temperature, humidity, surface temperature Do not coat where condensation risk violates instructions Material temperature Storage location and reading if required Condition materials within permitted range Forecast and door schedule Expected lows and planned openings Protect the cure period or reschedule The numbers must come from the exact products being installed. As one bounded example, the current Sikafloor-217 page shows different pot-life, foot-traffic, full-cure, and recoat times at 10°C, 20°C, and 30°C ( Sika product data ). Those values are not interchangeable with another epoxy, a polyaspartic, a repair mortar, or a primer. The example demonstrates why a generic “epoxy cures overnight” schedule is not a specification. Heating can create new variables Temporary heat should be treated as project equipment with a placement and monitoring plan. Settle these details before work: how long the space will be conditioned before preparation and application; whether equipment introduces combustion products or moisture; how fresh air will replace exhausted air without chilling the slab; who monitors conditions overnight; what happens during a power or heater failure; whether doors must open for vehicles, waste removal, or deliveries; how heaters and cords will be kept outside restricted or wet work areas. The goal is stable conditions, not the highest possible air temperature. Rapidly warming cold air can leave the concrete colder than the room. The crew should calculate and document the condensation margin required by the product data rather than relying on touch. Sequence winter logistics before mixing begins A workable Edmonton cold-weather sequence looks like this: Several days before: confirm the product-specific temperature range, arrange a safe enclosure, choose material storage, and review the forecast. Move vehicles, salt, snow, and wet mats away from the area. Before preparation: stabilize the room, inspect for water carried in by vehicles or melting snow, and measure the slab in a grid. Confirm dust-control equipment and safe exhaust routing. After preparation: prevent new condensation, tracked-in salt, or exhaust deposits from contaminating the open concrete. Recheck the substrate because preparation can reveal cracks, weak concrete, and damp areas. Before every layer: verify air, slab, humidity, and material conditions against that layer’s current product data sheet. Record batch numbers and application time so recoat decisions remain traceable. During cure: restrict doors, vehicles, washing, and foot traffic according to written criteria. Maintain the required conditions for the full period, not only until the crew leaves. Ventilation must still work in cold weather Closing every opening may conserve heat but does not substitute for an exposure-control plan. Health Canada recommends controlling pollutant sources, following label directions, and increasing ventilation during renovations ( Health Canada indoor-air guidance ). For an attached garage or occupied commercial space, ask where replacement air enters and where exhaust leaves. Check its relationship to doors, windows, soffits, and mechanical-air intakes. Identify who can enter the zone and what signs or barriers will be used. The product safety data sheets, not odour strength, should inform protective measures and occupancy decisions. Compare winter proposals on controls A credible cold-weather scope answers six questions in writing: Which exact products and product-data-sheet editions govern the work? What are the permitted air, slab, humidity, and condensation conditions for each layer? Who records those conditions, and can the owner see the log? How are materials stored and conditioned? How are heat and ventilation balanced safely? What is the contingency if conditions leave the permitted range? Do not accept a warmer-season timeline copied into a winter quote without these dependencies. The project may proceed, change products, need longer conditioning, or be postponed. A planned no-go decision is better than forcing a layer onto a slab that does not meet its written requirements. This guide does not set application temperatures or safe ventilation rates. Use the current product data and safety data sheets, applicable Alberta safety requirements, and qualified site-specific advice. Garage flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading Canadian Climate Normals 1991–2020: Edmonton City Environment and Climate Change Canada · Official Edmonton composite-station normals and extremes. Health Canada: Improve indoor air quality in your home Health Canada · Guidance for source control and ventilation during renovation work. Sikafloor-217 product data Sika Corporation · Bounded manufacturer example showing temperature-dependent pot life, cure, and recoat values; not a project recommendation. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/floor-coating-estimate-from-photos/
Floor Coating Estimate by Photo | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / planning planning · Edmonton floor library Floor Coating Estimate by Photo What photos to send for a free floor coating estimate in Edmonton: wide shots, cracks, stains, edges, drains, rough measurements, and what photos can't show. Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor Can you get a floor coating estimate from photos? Yes. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit, and for most garages and basements, good photos get most of the way to a real number. The photos have to show what drives the price: the size and shape of the floor, the condition of the concrete, the damage, and anything the coating has to work around. Here is what to send, how to take it, and what no photo can tell anyone. Start with the whole floor Clear what you can, even if only for the photos. A floor hidden under storage bins cannot be judged. Then take four wide shots: Two corner shots. Stand in one corner and photograph the floor to the far corner. Then do the opposite corner. Together they show the whole slab. From the doorway. For a garage, stand outside the open overhead door and shoot in. This shows the door strip, the parking tracks, and the slope toward the door or drain. From the back wall. Turn around and shoot toward the door. Shoot in daylight with the lights on. Avoid a flash pointed straight at the floor; it flattens texture and hides stains. Then the close-ups Close-ups show what the preparation and repairs will involve: Cracks. One wide shot to show where they run, then a close-up with a coin or a tape measure beside the widest point for scale. Stains. Oil under the engine bay, rust marks, and anything dark or shiny. Edges and damage. Chips at the door, broken edges, and spots where salt has scaled the surface. Old finishes. Paint, a sealer, or an old coating, especially where it is peeling. A close-up of a lifting edge says more than a paragraph. Drains, steps, and posts. Anything the coating has to stop at or wrap around. Signs of water. White powdery deposits, damp corners, or water marks along a wall. Add the numbers and the story Photos show the condition. A few facts fill in the rest: Rough measurements, wall to wall. How the space is used: parking, a workshop, a home gym, storage, or living space. Whether the space is heated, and whether the slab has in-floor heat. Any history of water, and whether the slab is new. The finish you are leaning toward. The finish library and the floor visualizer help if you are not sure yet. When you would like the floor done. A short video works too. Walk slowly, keep the floor in frame, and say what you know about it. What photos cannot show Photos show the surface. They do not show what is inside the slab. Three things usually need someone on site: Moisture. Moisture in concrete is measured, not seen. ASTM F2170 describes testing relative humidity inside the slab. A dry-looking floor in a photo does not rule it out. The bond of old coatings. Paint or an old coating can look sound and still come up in sheets once grinding starts. Hollow or weak concrete. Delaminated areas sound different when tapped. A camera cannot hear them. That is why an estimate from photos is a starting point for the scope, not a promise about every square metre. The surface preparation has to suit the coating system, as the ICRI guideline on surface preparation sets out, and some of that can only be confirmed on the floor. Photo mistakes that slow an estimate Most back-and-forth comes from a handful of habits: Only close-ups. A tight shot of a crack says nothing about where it runs or how much floor there is. Always send the wide shots first. No scale. A crack can look like a hairline or a canyon depending on the zoom. Put a coin, a pen, or a tape measure beside it. A covered floor. Bins, mats, and a parked car hide exactly what matters. Move what you can, even to one side. Night light. Warm bulbs turn grey concrete yellow and hide stains. Daylight through the open door is best for a garage. Blurry phones. Tap the screen to focus on the floor, hold still, and take two of each shot. When a visit is the better start Photos work well for most garages and basements. A visit is often the better first step when the floor is large or commercial, when there is a known water problem, when an old coating is peeling in patches, or when a new slab may have been sealed and nobody knows with what. It also helps when the space is hard to photograph, such as a long shop with poor light. You can ask for either; the estimate is free both ways. What a good estimate tells you back Whatever you send, the reply should be specific: the preparation the floor needs, which repairs are included, the system and finish proposed, what is not included, and what could change once the floor is ground. Alberta’s advice on hiring a contractor is to get estimates and changes in writing. Our guide to garage coating costs explains what moves the number, and the contractor questions guide lists what to ask next. Send them to Denis When the photos are ready, send them through the quote form or call (780) 991-1651. Say what the space is for and when you would like the floor done. You will hear what the photos show, and whether a visit would help before a firm quote. More on the work itself: residential epoxy flooring and commercial epoxy flooring . Questions people ask How many photos should I send for a floor coating estimate? Usually eight to twelve: two corner shots of the whole floor, one from the doorway, one from the back wall, and close-ups of cracks, stains, damaged edges, drains, and any old coating. A slow video walk-around can replace some of them. Do I need exact measurements? No. Rough wall-to-wall measurements are enough to start. Note anything that breaks the floor up, such as a step, a drain, or a curb, because edges and details take more time than open floor. Is an estimate from photos the final price? It is a starting point for the scope. Moisture, the bond of an old coating, and hollow concrete cannot be judged from a picture. Ask what the estimate assumes and what could change once the floor is ground or tested. Is the estimate free? Yes. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit, for garages, basements, shops, and commercial floors in Edmonton. Residential flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading Hiring a contractor Government of Alberta · Consumer guidance on written estimates, contracts, and changes. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Standard test for relative humidity inside a concrete slab. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Selecting and specifying concrete surface preparation for sealers, coatings, and overlays. Keep exploring Related floor guides Service: Surface Preparation ↗ Garage Coating Costs in Edmonton ↗ Floor Coating Site Assessment ↗ Ask Your Floor Coating Contractor ↗

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/floor-flake-colour-design-guide/
Floor Flake Colour Design Guide | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / planning planning · Edmonton floor library Floor Flake Colour Design Guide Design practical flake colour for Edmonton garage floors by lighting, dirt camouflage, slip needs, and how full-broadcast flake systems look day to day. Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor Start with the room, not the colour chart Floor flakes are small decorative chips, but their effect is architectural: they can make a floor read lighter or darker, busier or calmer. Begin with the real room. Note the walls, cabinets, overhead door, vehicles, equipment, natural light, and colour of the installed lighting. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . An Edmonton garage that looks bright on a summer afternoon can feel different under winter evening light. Carry shortlisted samples to several parts of the room and view them when the space is normally used. A phone photo helps comparison, but cameras automatically change exposure and white balance; let the eye make the final decision. Four controls create the appearance People often choose only a named blend. The finished result comes from four related decisions. Base colour. Gaps between chips may reveal the colour below. One blend can look different over another base. Blend composition. Chip colours, sizes, and proportions establish contrast and movement. A small strong accent can read differently across a full room than in a hand sample. Broadcast density. A lighter scatter leaves more base visible. A heavier broadcast makes chips dominant. Neither is automatically better; the proposal should describe the intended result and a system able to hold it. Clear finish and texture. Sheen, film build, and traction media affect reflection and surface relief. These are maintenance and use decisions as well as visual ones. Ask for a labelled sample identifying all four. Record the manufacturer’s colour or blend code in the proposal because informal names can be remembered differently. Design for what must remain visible A mottled, medium-contrast floor may make routine dust and small marks less visually dominant. It can also make small hardware, clear debris, or spills harder to see. A dark field may highlight pale winter residue; a light field may show tire soil. Test these observations instead of treating them as rules. If you work on equipment, place representative fasteners on the sample and view them from standing height. At stairs, ramps, or level changes, consider whether deliberate contrast is preferable to a continuous camouflage pattern. If parking guides or safety markings matter, decide whether they are in the coating scope or separate markings applied later. Run a consistent sample test Shortlist two or three options, then assess each the same way: Place the sample flat on the floor, not vertically in your hand. View it near the door, at the back wall, and beneath the main fixtures. Set wall paint, cabinet, trim, or tile samples beside it. Place a representative small object and a little clean grit on top. Look from the doorway and standing height, not only close up. Ask whether it still works if vehicles or wall colours change. For an appearance-sensitive project, discuss a larger mock-up made with the proposed layers and application method. Clarify whether it is a colour reference, texture reference, or both. Random chip placement means a sample cannot predict every detail of a full floor. Decoration cannot fix the slab Flakes do not bridge structural movement, correct drainage, stop moisture, or make weak concrete sound. The ACI concrete-repair guide treats evaluation, repair, preparation, and protective systems as connected work. Choose colour alongside a concrete assessment, never instead of one. Repairs may remain perceptible, especially under directional light. Ask how joints will be treated and whether they remain visible. The guide to cracks and spalling under coatings frames that conversation. If moisture testing is specified, ASTM F2170 is one recognized in-situ relative-humidity method, but the product manufacturer’s current limits must govern acceptance. Texture, cleaning, and repairs More surface relief may change traction but gives soil more texture around which to collect. A smoother finish may wipe more easily yet feel different when wet. Tell the contractor whether the floor sees meltwater, oily work, rolling stools, bare feet, or mobility aids. No colour or flake pattern guarantees slip resistance; contaminants, footwear, cleaning, wear, and slope matter. Use the slip-resistance planning guide to document actual conditions. Request care instructions for the complete finish and confirm acceptable cleaners, pads, brushes, and snow-removal tools. Retain exact codes, product names, the approved sample, and project photographs. A later repair may differ because of batch variation, aging, gloss, and random chip placement. Ask whether a natural boundary such as a joint offers the most practical repair limit. Put the final choice into a room record Take one photograph of every candidate in the same location and light, then record why the chosen option won. Note any accent colour that must remain visible, the desired contrast at edges, and whether the priority is hiding routine soil or making it easy to see. This brief gives the installer more useful direction than “we liked the grey one.” Have every decision-maker approve the same physical sample. If two adjoining rooms are coated at different times, clarify whether colour continuity or an intentional transition is expected and where the boundary falls. Keep one dated sample with the project record so later questions refer to the same physical standard, not a screen image or memory. Before approval, have the proposal state base colour, blend code, broadcast description, clear-coat type, intended texture, and reference sample. Garage flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · A current ACI guide covering concrete repair, protection, preparation, and quality control. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Check the current edition and the specified test procedure. Keep exploring Related floor guides Service: Decorative Epoxy ↗ Cracks and Spalling Before Coat ↗ Slip Resistance in Floor Coatings ↗

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/garage-floor-preparation-edmonton/
Garage Floor Prep in Edmonton | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / preparation preparation · Edmonton floor library Garage Floor Prep in Edmonton Follow Edmonton garage floor preparation steps: cleaning, oil treatment, repairs, and diamond grinding so flake or solid epoxy sits on a profiled slab. Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor Preparation begins before equipment arrives A sound preparation plan identifies the slab’s condition, contaminants, previous treatments, repairs, joints, moisture questions, drainage, and edges before selecting a machine. Edmonton garages add a familiar use pattern: vehicles carry meltwater, grit, and de-icing residue; the doorway may be colder than the wall shared with the house; drains and parking tracks form distinct exposure zones. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Those conditions do not dictate one system. They tell the assessor where to look. Read the garage zone by zone Clear enough belongings to expose the concrete. Divide the floor into parking tracks, doorway band, perimeter, drain area, work zone, cracks, and old patches. Photograph concerns from a wide view and close up. Look for dark or oily areas, white deposits, scaling, weak concrete, old paint or sealer, crack and patch boundaries, low spots, and water-entry points. The Alberta Infrastructure bulletin on de-icing concrete discusses de-icers, saturation, freeze-thaw exposure, and spring washing. Although written for infrastructure, it supports a useful garage principle: winter residue is a condition to remove and assess, not coat over. Cleaning is not profiling Cleaning targets soluble, greasy, or loose contamination. Mechanical profiling changes the concrete surface to meet the coating specification. One cannot automatically substitute for the other. Grinding through visible oil, for example, does not by itself prove that remaining concrete is suitable. Ask for the sequence in suspect areas: how loose material will be removed, what cleaning chemistry will be used, how residue will be extracted, and what acceptance check follows. See oil-stain preparation questions for a focused checklist. Mechanical work may use diamond grinding, shot blasting, or another method chosen for the slab and system. The machine name alone is not a specification. Access, old material, edges, desired profile, dust control, and product instructions all matter. The ACI concrete-repair guide places surface preparation within evaluation, repair, material selection, and quality control: a helpful model for the full process. Specify and inspect the profile The coating manufacturer should define an acceptable prepared surface. Ask which current technical data sheet governs and how completion will be assessed. A floor can look clean while retaining weak laitance, embedded contamination, or an unsuitable profile. Edges, corners, curbs, posts, steps, drains, and the strip under the overhead door need explicit treatment because large machines reach them differently. The proposal should name the smaller tools used and state where the coating terminates. Our diamond-grinding guide expands on equipment, dust collection, and edge work. Repairs follow exposure Preparation can reveal defects hidden by dirt or an old finish. Include a decision point: who reviews newly exposed cracks or unsound concrete, who authorizes added repairs, and how scope or schedule changes are approved. Cracks should not all receive one automatic treatment. Ask whether movement is suspected and whether the cause is understood. Control and construction joints may need to keep functioning rather than being rigidly covered. Spalls require sound boundaries and a compatible repair sequence. Repair materials must fit the coating manufacturer’s application and recoat requirements. Treat moisture as an evidence question Past efflorescence, damp edges, dark areas, or known drainage problems may justify investigation. A coating is not a drainage repair. Ask what moisture information the manufacturer requires, which test is proposed, where tests will be placed, and how results change the system choice. Avoid treating one casual meter reading as universal clearance. Instruments and test methods answer different questions. The concrete moisture testing guide outlines records worth requesting: method, location, date, conditions, result, and the selected product’s limit. Plan the work around the household Preparation produces construction noise and dust. Confirm containment, collection equipment, ventilation, power, waste handling, and the route for equipment. Ask how the home is separated from the garage and whether the overhead door must remain open. Weather can affect that plan, so a calendar date should never override the ambient and substrate conditions in current product documents. Discuss freezers, appliances, fixed cabinets, stairs, and objects fastened to the slab. Clarify who disconnects or moves them, where stored items and vehicles go, and whether coating beneath equipment is included. Establish a pre-coating hold point Before liquid material is mixed, the crew should confirm completed preparation and repairs, clean edges, acceptable slab condition, correct products, and the environmental conditions required by their data sheets. Photographs create a useful baseline. Any departure from the written scope should be approved before it disappears beneath the floor system. Photograph the condition that will disappear Prepared concrete and completed repairs are soon hidden. Request overview photographs after belongings are removed, close-ups after profiling, and a final set before primer or body coat. The record should show cracks, joints, drain edges, doorway band, repaired areas, and any accepted exception. Photographs do not prove every technical requirement, but they make scope changes and later troubleshooting easier to understand. Pair them with the named product documents and recorded site conditions rather than using appearance as the only acceptance test. Ask the final proposal to identify preparation method, special-treatment areas, repair allowances or exclusions, edges and drains, dust controls, moisture plan, and the person who accepts the substrate. This sequence is a planning framework, not a project method statement. Garage flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading Alberta Infrastructure: De-Icing Concrete Government of Alberta · Technical bulletin on de-icers, concrete durability, and spring washing. ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Concrete repair and protective-system selection guidance. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/hot-tire-pickup-epoxy/
Hot-Tire Pickup on Epoxy Floors | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / maintenance maintenance · Edmonton floor library Hot-Tire Pickup on Epoxy Floors Troubleshoot hot-tire pickup on Edmonton epoxy garage floors with prep, topcoat, and cure questions focused on evidence, not invented one-day install claims. Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor First confirm what actually happened “Hot-tire pickup” is commonly used for damage or marking beneath tires, but the label is not a diagnosis. A dark tire imprint on top of a coating is different from softened film, a separated top layer, or a coating stack that has lifted to bare concrete. The repair depends on which condition exists. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Avoid aggressive scrubbing, sanding, or spot coating before documentation. Move the vehicle if it can be done without enlarging damage, then photograph the whole parking bay, all four tire positions, close details with scale, and an unaffected comparison area. Side lighting can reveal raised edges or loss of film. Create a simple incident record Write down the date, vehicle and tire position, length of the drive before parking, weather, garage conditions, how long the vehicle remained, recent cleaning, and when the floor was installed or last recoated. Record whether the same tire position is affected repeatedly and whether another vehicle causes the same pattern. Collect the proposal, warranty, product data sheets, maintenance instructions, application photos, batch information supplied at handover, and previous correspondence. Do not assume every layer is epoxy; many decorative systems combine different material categories. Read the damage from top to bottom An assessor should determine where separation occurred: residue sitting on an intact topcoat; damage within the topcoat; separation between coating layers; separation between coating and primer; separation at the concrete surface; weak concrete attached to the underside of the removed film. That boundary directs the investigation. If concrete remains attached, substrate strength may be relevant. If layers separated cleanly, recoat timing, surface condition, contamination, or compatibility may need review. If the surface only carries a mark, start with the manufacturer’s approved cleaning procedure rather than a repair assumption. The ACI concrete-repair guide addresses condition assessment, surface preparation, repair, and quality control. It does not diagnose this specific floor, but it supports examining the complete substrate-and-system chain instead of blaming a product category from appearance alone. Possible lines of inquiry, not conclusions A useful assessment may consider concrete condition, mechanical preparation, oil or sealer contamination, moisture, repairs, primer selection, layer compatibility, mixing, film thickness, recoat windows, ambient and slab conditions, cure protection, vehicle return timing, cleaning chemistry, and tire exposure. Each hypothesis needs evidence. A statement that “the tires were hot” does not establish the failure mechanism. Neither does a statement that “epoxy always does this.” Request the applicable manufacturer documents and compare actual job records with their requirements. Moisture deserves proportionate consideration when the pattern or slab history suggests it. ASTM F2170 defines one in-situ concrete relative-humidity method, but a new test cannot reconstruct every condition present at installation. It should be interpreted with slab history, product limits, and other observations. What to do while the issue is open Keep the area clean and dry using only documented care methods. Avoid parking repeatedly on a loose edge, dragging tools over it, or applying tape that could pull more film. Mark the boundary lightly outside the damage or use dated photographs to see whether it changes. Contact the installer promptly through the process described in the warranty. Provide the incident record rather than only a close-up image. Ask whether they want the area left untouched for inspection and whether continued vehicle use could affect the assessment. The related guide on tire pickup across floor-coating systems helps prepare neutral questions, while floor-coating warranty questions explains the records and notice steps to check. Evaluate a proposed repair A repair scope should state how the affected boundary will be found, what is removed, how concrete and remaining coating are prepared, which layers are replaced, how compatibility is established, and what visual difference may remain. It should also address why the cause is considered localized and what evidence supports returning the same system to that area. Ask about colour, flake, and gloss variation. A technically sound localized repair may remain visible because the surrounding floor has aged and decorative broadcast is random. Natural boundaries such as joints may offer a clearer stopping point. Questions for the inspection meeting Ask the assessor to show you the failure plane and explain what observation supports it. Then ask: Is the condition residue, cohesive damage, or loss of bond? Is concrete attached to the removed coating? Does the pattern align only with tire contact or extend beyond it? Which installation and maintenance records were reviewed? Which alternative causes were considered and ruled out? Does the proposed repair address a cause or only restore appearance? Request a short written finding even if the conclusion remains uncertain. “Insufficient evidence” can be an honest result and may point to monitoring or broader sampling. Avoid allowing a tiny destructive test without first agreeing how the test area will be restored. If parking positions differ, label samples and photographs carefully; mixing locations can erase the pattern an assessor needs. Note unaffected tires too, because absence at a comparable position helps frame the investigation. Finally, obtain separate restrictions for walking, vehicle return, cleaning, and chemical exposure. Do not turn a generic cure statement into an exact schedule. This guide preserves evidence and improves the conversation; it cannot determine cause from a description alone. Residential flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · A current ACI guide covering concrete repair, protection, preparation, and quality control. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Check the current edition and the specified test procedure. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/how-to-clean-coated-garage-floor/
How to Clean Coated Garage Floors | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / maintenance maintenance · Edmonton floor library How to Clean Coated Garage Floors Clean a coated Edmonton garage floor without harsh guesswork: winter salt rinse habits, mild detergents, and care that protects flake or solid epoxy topcoats. Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor The reliable routine: dry soil first, wet cleaning second Loose grit behaves like an abrasive under shoes, tires, rolling cabinets, and snow-removal tools. Begin by removing it with a soft broom, dust mop, or vacuum tool approved for the finish. Work from the back of the garage toward the door and pay attention to flake texture, edges, corners, parking tracks, and drains. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Only then move to wet cleaning. Start with the coating manufacturer’s maintenance instructions, including cleaner type, dilution, water temperature, dwell time, agitation tool, rinsing, and drying. If those instructions are missing, request them before experimenting. “Epoxy-safe” on a retail label does not prove compatibility with the actual topcoat. A practical wash sequence Move vehicles and portable belongings; protect anything that cannot get wet. Photograph unusual stains, loose edges, blisters, or cracks before cleaning. Sweep or vacuum thoroughly. Pre-treat only with a product and concentration accepted by the coating supplier. Apply the maintenance solution in manageable sections. Agitate with the approved soft brush or pad without letting dirty solution dry. Pick up the solution or direct it only where drainage and local rules allow. Rinse if the product instructions require it, then remove standing water. Let the floor dry and inspect from several angles. Change dirty water rather than spreading it. Cleaner residue can leave haze or create a different walking feel, so rinsing and recovery matter where specified. Edmonton winter soil needs seasonal attention Meltwater can carry grit and de-icing residue into parking tracks and the doorway band. Use trays or mats only if their backing and placement are compatible with the coating, and lift them periodically to inspect and clean beneath them. The Alberta Infrastructure de-icing concrete bulletin discusses salt scaling, saturation, and freeze-thaw exposure and recommends thoroughly washing concrete surfaces exposed to de-icers each spring. A coated residential garage is not the bulletin’s infrastructure application, but the maintenance cue is useful: do not allow accumulated winter residue to become the default condition. Follow the coating maker’s wash method and manage rinse water appropriately. Match the response to the spill For fresh oil or automotive fluid, contain and lift the material promptly with methods allowed by the maintenance guide. Avoid spreading it across a larger area. Consult both the fluid label or safety data sheet and coating instructions before choosing a cleaner. Ventilate as directed and keep ignition sources and incompatible chemicals away. For rubber marks or unidentified dark streaks, begin with the mildest approved method. A mark on top is not the same as coating softened or pulled from the slab. If film is lifting beneath a tire, stop cleaning and use the hot-tire pickup documentation guide . For paint, adhesive, rust-coloured deposits, or construction residue, do not reach immediately for solvent, a razor, or an abrasive pad. Ask the coating supplier for a compatible method. Scraping can cut the finish, while solvents can change gloss or soften some materials. Tools and products to question before use Confirm compatibility before using concentrated degreasers, citrus cleaners, bleach mixtures, acids, solvents, powdered abrasives, steam, pressure washers, stiff wire brushes, or aggressive machine pads. Never mix cleaning chemicals. Product labels, safety data sheets, ventilation requirements, and disposal instructions still apply even when a cleaner is accepted for the floor. If a pressure washer or autoscrubber is proposed, request limits for pressure, nozzle, distance, pad, brush, and water recovery. Edges, joints, damaged areas, and transitions may need gentler treatment. Test an unfamiliar approved method in an inconspicuous area and let it dry before judging gloss or colour. Inspect while you clean Cleaning is the best time to note changes. Keep a dated photograph if you find a chip, crack, blister, cloudy area, worn texture, or separation at an edge. Mark its location on a simple garage sketch and compare it at the next cleaning. Do not coat over, grind, or aggressively probe a questionable area before the installer sees it, especially if warranty notice may apply. The ACI concrete-repair guide treats condition assessment, preparation, repair, and quality control as connected work: a useful reason to document before changing the evidence. The floor-coating warranty guide lists records and claim-process questions to preserve. Build a maintenance card Keep a one-page card with the system and topcoat name, approved routine cleaner and dilution, allowed tools, prohibited products, spill contact, and installer details. Store the current manufacturer instructions with project documents. This prevents a future owner, cleaner, or employee from guessing. Diagnose haze before cleaning again If a dry floor looks cloudy, compare an untouched area, a rinsed test area, and the normal walking path. Haze may be residue, fine scratching, moisture beneath a temporary covering, or a change in the coating. Repeating stronger cleaning without knowing which can make the evidence harder to read. Photograph the condition in side light and ask the installer which approved test distinguishes residue from film change. If the maintenance method is responsible, update the cleaning card so another person does not repeat it. If the coating appears soft, loose, or blistered, restrict the area and request an assessment. Date the maintenance card whenever an instruction changes, the floor is recoated, or a cleaner is approved. Frequency should follow actual soil rather than a universal calendar. Sweep when grit is present, address spills promptly, and schedule fuller washing around winter accumulation and workspace use. Dispose of cleaning products and recovered water according to the label and applicable local requirements. Garage flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading Alberta Infrastructure: De-Icing Concrete Government of Alberta · Technical bulletin on de-icers, concrete durability, and spring washing. ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Concrete repair and protective-system selection guidance. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/new-concrete-before-floor-coating/
New Concrete Before Floor Coating | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / preparation preparation · Edmonton floor library New Concrete Before Floor Coating Coating a new garage floor in Edmonton: why new concrete needs time, curing versus drying, curing compounds, laitance, moisture tests, and builder questions. Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor How long should new concrete wait before it is coated? Long enough to cure, and to dry to the coating’s limit. New concrete gains strength over weeks, and it holds a lot of water while it does. Coating manufacturers set a minimum age and a moisture limit for their products, and a moisture test confirms the slab has reached it. On a new-build garage, that often means the coating goes down well after move-in. It is worth the wait. A coating applied over a slab that is still wet can trap that moisture, then blister or lose its bond. Curing and drying are not the same thing Curing is the chemical reaction that hardens concrete. It needs water and time, and it carries on for weeks after the pour. The ACI guide to curing covers how curing is done and why it matters for strength and surface quality. Drying is the slab giving up the extra water that was needed to place and finish it. A slab can be well cured and still too wet for a coating. That is why a moisture test is the real gate, not the calendar. ASTM F2170 describes measuring relative humidity inside the slab, and the product documents say what reading is acceptable. Our moisture testing guide explains the options. What the builder may have put on the surface New slabs often get a curing compound or a sealer sprayed on after finishing. It helps the concrete cure. It also stops a coating from bonding, so it has to come off, and it is not always visible. Ask your builder what was applied, and keep the answer for your coating contractor. New floors can also carry a weak, powdery top layer called laitance, left when water and fine material rise to the surface during finishing. It can look smooth and solid, but a coating bonded to it is only as strong as that thin layer. Grinding removes it. The ICRI guideline on surface preparation explains why the prepared surface has to suit the coating system, and new concrete is no exception. The finish on the slab matters too Garage slabs are often trowelled to a smooth, dense finish. That surface is easy to sweep and hard for a coating to grip until it is ground open. A broom finish is rougher, but it can still carry laitance. Either way, the preparation is diamond grinding, and the surface profile guide explains what an open surface means in practice. The diamond grinding guide covers the equipment. Cracks and joints in a new slab New concrete shrinks as it dries. That is why slabs have control joints, cuts that give the shrinkage a place to crack neatly. Hairline cracks in the first months are common and usually cosmetic. The ACI guide to floor and slab construction explains shrinkage, curling, and joint spacing. For a coating, the useful questions are simple. Are the cracks stable, or still moving? Where are the joints, and will the coating bridge them or stop at them? Cosmetic crack filling is part of the preparation. A crack that keeps growing is a question for the builder first. Why the wait pays off Waiting feels like lost time when the garage is right there. The alternative costs more. A coating over wet concrete can blister as moisture pushes up under it, or let go in patches where it never bonded properly. Fixing that means grinding the failed coating off and starting again, on a floor that now has to be prepared twice. A few extra weeks before the first coat is the cheaper path. Living with the slab before it is coated If you move in before the floor is coated, a few habits keep the concrete ready for it: Catch drips. Oil and fluids soak into new concrete fast. A drip tray under each vehicle saves grinding later. The oil stain guide explains why soaked-in oil is hard to remove. Rinse out the salt. In the first winter, sweep and rinse meltwater and road salt out of the garage rather than letting it dry on the floor. Skip the sealer. If you plan to coat, ask the builder not to add a sealer or hardener on top, or at least to tell you exactly what went on. Avoid rubber mats and tape. Some leave residue or stains that have to be ground away. A new-build checklist Before booking a coating on new concrete, gather: The pour date. What curing compound, sealer, or hardener was applied, if any. Whether the slab has in-floor heat. See coating a heated garage floor . Any cracks, and whether they have changed. Whether a moisture test has been done, when, and the result. Plan early, book later You can choose a finish, get an estimate, and plan the timing long before the slab is ready. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit, so a new-build garage can be quoted as soon as it is clear. Send photos and the pour date through the quote form , and read about garage floor coating in Edmonton . Questions people ask How long do I have to wait to coat a new concrete floor? Until the slab meets the coating's minimum age and moisture limit. The product's documents set both, and a moisture test confirms the slab is ready. The calendar alone is not the test, because drying depends on the slab, the weather, and the space. Is the white film on my new garage floor a problem? It may be a curing compound, a sealer, or efflorescence. Curing compounds and sealers stop a coating from bonding and have to be removed by grinding. Ask your builder what was applied and pass the answer on to your contractor. Are cracks in a new garage floor normal? Hairline shrinkage cracks are common as new concrete dries, which is why slabs have control joints. Cosmetic cracks are filled before coating. A crack that keeps widening is a question for the builder first. Can I get an estimate before the new concrete is ready? Yes. You can choose a finish and get an estimate from photos early, then book the install once the slab has cured and tested dry enough for the product. Garage flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-308-16: Guide to External Curing of Concrete American Concrete Institute · Curing practices, materials, and monitoring. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Standard test for relative humidity inside a concrete slab. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Selecting and specifying concrete surface preparation for sealers, coatings, and overlays. ACI PRC-302.1-15: Guide to Concrete Floor and Slab Construction American Concrete Institute · Floor and slab construction, shrinkage, cracking, and curling. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/remove-oil-stains-before-floor-coating/
Oil Stains Before Floor Coating | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / preparation preparation · Edmonton floor library Oil Stains Before Floor Coating Handle oil stains before Edmonton garage floor coating with cleaning, verification, and diamond-grind prep so epoxy flake systems are not coating over oil. Updated September 18, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor Oil on a garage floor is more than a dark mark. It can be contamination at the surface, liquid held in pores, or evidence of an active vehicle or equipment leak. A coating decision should begin by finding out which condition you have. Covering the stain before resolving that question can hide useful evidence and makes it harder to write a defensible preparation scope. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . For an Edmonton garage, start with a simple history. Mark where vehicles normally park, where snow melt collects, which stains are recent, what cleaners were used, and whether the area still feels greasy after drying. Photograph the floor in even light. A few notes now give the assessor more than a freshly washed slab with no context. Stop the source before treating the concrete Fix or contain the leak first. Otherwise, freshly prepared concrete can be contaminated again while the project is being planned. Move leaking equipment to a tray, address the vehicle problem, and keep oily rags or absorbent materials off the slab. If an unknown liquid may be hazardous, follow the product label and local disposal requirements rather than treating it as ordinary wash water. Do not mix cleaners or improvise with solvents. The relevant cleaner, dwell time, agitation, rinsing, recovery, and disposal method depend on the contaminant and the coating manufacturer’s written instructions. A contractor should be able to describe the process without promising that every old stain will disappear visually. Cleaning and mechanical preparation do different jobs Cleaning is intended to remove oil, grease, residue, and cleaning products. Mechanical preparation changes the concrete surface so the specified system can bond to it. One is not a substitute for the other. Grinding or blasting an oily slab can spread contamination, load tooling, or drive residue into adjacent areas; coating over a detergent film creates another problem. The sequence matters. The ACI concrete repair guide is a primary industry reference that covers condition assessment, surface preparation, repair materials, protective systems, and quality control. Its scope supports treating contamination as part of an evaluated concrete-repair process, not as a cosmetic cleaning step. The project specification and current product data sheets still control the actual method. An assessment may divide the floor into zones: sound, apparently clean concrete; visible staining that no longer transfers residue; areas that still release oil after cleaning; cracked, scaled, or previously patched concrete; an old coating with unknown adhesion or contamination beneath it. That map helps prevent a single preparation method from being applied blindly across the whole garage. What can show that the floor is ready? There is no universal household test that proves oily concrete is coatable. Ask what acceptance check the installer and coating manufacturer require. Depending on the written system, that may include visual inspection, checking for residue after cleaning, a small trial area, surface-profile verification, or an adhesion-related check. The important point is to agree on the evidence before the coating arrives, including who decides whether a questionable zone proceeds, receives more preparation, or is excluded. Moisture is a separate question. Darkening caused by oil does not establish the slab’s moisture condition, and a dry-looking surface is not a moisture test. ASTM F2170 describes in-situ relative-humidity testing in concrete floor slabs. When the selected manufacturer requires slab-moisture information, the proposal should name the required test method, timing, locations, and acceptance criteria rather than using oil cleanup as a proxy. If the garage also has scaling, spalls, or cracks around the contaminated area, review the guide to concrete cracks and spalling before coating before comparing repair allowances. Repairs need compatible preparation and cure conditions of their own. Questions that make a quotation clearer Invite the estimator to be specific. Useful questions include: Which areas are considered contaminated, and how will they be isolated from clean concrete? Which cleaner or treatment is proposed, and does its manufacturer permit the intended use? How will spent cleaner, oily water, and debris be contained and disposed of? What mechanical preparation follows cleaning? What result must be observed before primer or coating is applied? What happens if oil returns during preparation? Are deeply affected areas repairable within the quoted scope, or does work pause for a revised decision? Which current product data sheet governs surface condition, moisture, mixing, and application? A useful proposal distinguishes included work from contingencies. “Degrease as required” leaves the most important decision undefined. A better scope identifies the observed zones, planned sequence, acceptance check, and process for concealed conditions. What homeowners can do before the visit Avoid applying sealers, paint, acid, or a new degreaser immediately before the assessment. Keep the floor accessible, but leave enough evidence for the contractor to see the stain pattern. Gather the names of products previously used and, if available, the old coating or patch records. Note whether water beads, darkens the concrete unevenly, or carries an oily sheen after cleaning; report those observations without treating them as pass/fail tests. Edmonton winters add tracked de-icer, sand, water, and road grime to the mix. These are not all “oil,” and they may require different cleaning or repair decisions. The companion guide to winter salt and concrete-floor damage helps separate seasonal deposits from scaling or other concrete deterioration. The practical goal is not a perfectly colourless slab. It is a documented surface condition that the specified coating system permits. Until the contamination, concrete condition, moisture requirements, and acceptance checks are known, the responsible answer is to keep the scope open rather than turn a complex substrate issue into a blanket performance promise. Garage flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · A current ACI guide covering concrete repair, protection, preparation, and quality control. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Check the current edition and the specified test procedure. Keep exploring Related floor guides Service: Surface Preparation ↗ Winter Salt and Concrete Floors ↗ How to Clean Coated Garage Floors ↗

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/tire-pickup-floor-coatings/
Garage Tire Pickup: Causes Guide | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / maintenance maintenance · Edmonton floor library Garage Tire Pickup: Causes Guide Understand tire pickup on Edmonton garage floor coatings: heat, cure, topcoat, and prep questions that guide fixes without promising one-day install miracles. Updated September 18, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor Tire pickup describes coating that softens, lifts, tears, or transfers at the tire contact area. It is different from a rubber mark sitting on top of an intact finish. Before choosing a cleaner, repair, or replacement, establish which condition is present and what the floor system actually is. This guide covers prevention and causes across garage floor coating systems generally; if tire damage has already appeared on a specific epoxy floor, the hot-tire pickup diagnosis guide walks through the incident record and repair evaluation for that situation. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Read the pattern like evidence Photograph each parking position before cleaning. Mark front and rear tires, vehicle type, normal arrival time, and whether damage occurs after long drives. Record washing, heated tires, winter de-icer, oil, plasticizers from mats, and previous touch-ups. Note whether the edge is bonded, curled, soft, or exposing concrete. A black transfer mark that cleans off with a manufacturer-permitted method is not proof of coating failure. Conversely, repeated lifting at tire footprints deserves more than another spot of paint. Preserve loose pieces and product records for assessment. Prevention begins below the finish Concrete must be sound, clean, and prepared for the complete specified system. Oil, weak laitance, an unknown sealer, moisture conditions, or inadequate profile can undermine adhesion independently of tire heat. The ACI concrete repair guide covers evaluation, surface preparation, repair, protective systems, and quality control. That framework supports connecting a failure to substrate evidence rather than diagnosing it from the word “epoxy.” Ask the proposal to name the preparation method, edge work, repair materials, inspection point, and target surface condition. If oil staining is present, use the oil-contamination planning guide before mechanical preparation. Cleaning and profiling solve different problems. Product family is not a specification Different primers, body coats, broadcasts, and topcoats have different written requirements. Ask the manufacturer or installer for current product data sheets covering approved substrates, preparation, environmental limits, mixing, layer thickness, recoat timing, cure stages, chemical exposure, cleaning, and vehicle return. Make sure all layers are intended to work together. Avoid claims such as “hot-tire proof” unless the exact meaning, conditions, evidence, and limits are documented and approved for publication. A sample panel cannot reproduce every slab, vehicle, tire, parking pattern, or cure condition. Moisture is its own checkpoint A dry surface or successful blasting does not establish internal slab moisture. ASTM F2170 describes in-situ relative-humidity testing in concrete floor slabs. If the selected system requires that method, the scope should identify test locations, timing, reporting, and the product-specific limit. A moisture result informs selection; it does not guarantee performance under tires. Cure needs staged language “Dry” can refer to touch, foot traffic, light loads, chemical exposure, or full service. The contractor should provide written restrictions for walking, storage, washing, vehicle parking, mats, and normal use. Conditions in a garage near an Edmonton overhead door can differ from those at the centre of the slab, so record air and substrate conditions as the manufacturer requires. Do not rush vehicles back based on a generic number from another product. Keep the floor clean and protected during the cure period. If a vehicle must enter sooner than permitted, that is a scheduling conflict to resolve before application, not after. If damage already exists Stop parking on soft or lifting zones where practical. Do not pull loose edges to “see how far it goes.” Photograph, clean only as permitted, and ask for an assessment that maps bonded and unbonded areas. A local repair may remain visible and is reasonable only when the cause, boundary, preparation, and compatibility are addressed. Widespread failure, unknown materials, repeated patches, dampness, or contamination may point to broader removal. The repair-or-replace assessment explains how to compare local repair, recoat, and replacement scopes. Questions for a garage-coating quote What observed conditions create tire-pickup risk here? Which exact layers are proposed, and where are their current data sheets? How will oil, old coatings, sealers, repairs, and edges be handled? What preparation acceptance check occurs before primer? What moisture information does this system require? What environmental records are kept during application and cure? When are foot traffic, washing, mats, and vehicles permitted? How would a tire-contact repair be evaluated and blended? Tire pickup is not prevented by a resin label alone. It is managed through condition assessment, substrate preparation, compatible layers, controlled application, adequate cure, and responsible use. Add seasonal maintenance to the plan Vehicle areas need routine observation after handover. Sweep or vacuum grit before wet cleaning, remove de-icer residue with a manufacturer-permitted method, and contain new leaks promptly. Check tire positions, door thresholds, drain edges, cracks, and repair boundaries during cleaning. Avoid sharp metal tools, unapproved solvents, and aggressive pads. Keep mats or trays only when both their manufacturer and the coating documentation support the intended contact. Lift them periodically when permitted to inspect for trapped moisture, residue, or marking. Do not leave an unknown rubber or plastic backing on a new finish simply because it is sold as garage protection. Create a small log with photographs at handover, after the first winter, and whenever the vehicle or use changes. Record cleaners, tools, spills, and unusual marks. Early evidence helps distinguish a removable transfer from developing adhesion loss. It also gives a contractor useful context before a repair spreads beyond the original tire position. If parking changes to a heavier vehicle, different tire type, frequent long-distance arrival, or equipment with concentrated wheels, disclose that change and request a new product-specific review. The installed system was selected for documented conditions, not every future garage use. Garage flake floors Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · A current ACI guide covering concrete repair, protection, preparation, and quality control. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Check the current edition and the specified test procedure. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/when-to-move-furniture-back-coated-floor/
When to Move Furniture Back On | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / planning planning · Edmonton floor library When to Move Furniture Back On When to Move Furniture Back On. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/winter-salt-concrete-floor-damage/
Winter Salt and Concrete Floors | Final Finish Epoxy

Home / Resources / maintenance maintenance · Edmonton floor library Winter Salt and Concrete Floors Limit winter salt damage on Edmonton concrete floors with rinse habits, garage prep awareness, and repair-or-coat decisions grounded in real slab condition. Updated September 18, 2026 Ask Denis about a flake floor Edmonton winters bring meltwater, grit, and de-icing chemicals onto garage, parkade, loading, and entrance floors. The visible white residue is only part of the story. Water movement, repeated wetting, freezing exposure at edges, existing cracks, and concrete quality all affect what you see. A coating is not a substitute for diagnosing and repairing deteriorated concrete. For local scope options, see our Surface Preparation . Read the official Alberta guidance first Alberta Infrastructure’s technical bulletin on de-icing concrete discusses de-icer effects on concrete and calls for thorough spring washing of treated concrete. Use that primary source to frame seasonal care, while following site requirements for containment and discharge. Do not send salty or contaminated wash water to a drain without confirming it is permitted. The bulletin is not a project-specific repair specification. Interior heated slabs, exposed aprons, ramps, and thresholds experience different water and temperature conditions. Make a winter condition map Before deep cleaning, photograph tire paths, door lines, drains, joints, wall edges, ramps, and wet spots. Mark: loose or flaking surface material; shallow scaling or deeper spalls; cracks and displaced edges; rust staining or exposed metal; white deposits and persistent dampness; hollow or failed patches; damage at the warm-to-cold transition; routes where vehicles or footwear deposit slurry. Repeat photographs after cleaning and drying. Appearance alone cannot establish depth or cause, but the pattern helps an assessor distinguish deposits from material loss and choose investigation points. Control water and tracked material Repair leaks and review drainage, door seals, downspouts, grading, and snow-storage practices with appropriate trades. Remove standing water promptly using a method suitable for the facility. Entrance mats and containment can reduce tracking but need cleaning and drying so they do not become saturated reservoirs. Sweep or vacuum grit before wet cleaning to reduce abrasion. Use cleaners and equipment permitted for the concrete or installed coating. Never mix cleaning products. Follow labels and safety data sheets, protect occupants, and manage runoff. Damaged concrete needs a repair decision Soundness, contamination, cracks, reinforcing corrosion, joints, and moisture must be evaluated before coating. The ACI PRC-546 concrete repair guide covers evaluation, concrete removal, preparation, repair materials, protective systems, and quality control. That primary framework supports mapping deterioration and selecting repairs before a protective finish. Deep spalling, exposed or corroded reinforcement, significant displacement, structural concern, or continuing water entry may require an engineer or other qualified professional. Do not fill a moving joint or unstable spall simply to create a flat decorative surface. The concrete cracks and spalling guide helps organize observations for an assessment. Ask how repair edges are cut or prepared, how unsound material is identified, which repair product is compatible, and what cure occurs before coating. Coating selection starts after evaluation Request the complete layer sequence and current manufacturer requirements for substrate, preparation, moisture, temperature, application, cure, chemical exposure, and cleaning. Ask which winter exposures the recommendation is intended to address and which remain owner controls. Avoid blanket claims that a coating is “salt proof” or will stop freeze-thaw damage. The result depends on the exact system, concrete, detailing, exposure, defects, and maintenance. A coating also cannot correct drainage or stop water entering from an unresolved source. At door thresholds and ramps, define terminations deliberately. Snowplows, shovels, tire chains, metal edges, and abrupt transitions may create mechanical damage that needs operational controls or sacrificial details. Plan seasonal maintenance at handover The owner should receive approved cleaning products, dilution, tools, frequency, spill response, inspection points, and prohibited methods. Include a spring inspection after accumulated winter material is removed. Look for chips, worn texture, lifting edges, cracks, dampness, and damaged terminations. Document changes early. A small local repair may be possible when the boundary is sound and compatibility is known; repeated or widespread damage needs a broader diagnosis. Keep the winter log with product and repair records. Bring these questions to the quotation Which observed areas show deposits, scaling, spalling, moisture, or previous repair? What additional assessment is needed before a coating scope? How will de-icer, oil, old coatings, and weak concrete be handled? Which cracks, joints, drains, ramps, and thresholds are included? What inspection proves the substrate is ready for the specified system? What winter cleaning and runoff plan is compatible with the finish? Which damage requires prompt review after installation? Winter salt is a recurring exposure to manage, not a single stain to cover. A defensible Edmonton plan connects source control, cleaning, concrete repair, coating documents, and seasonal inspection. Distinguish the heated floor from the exposed edge An interior garage bay, overhead-door line, exterior apron, ramp, and wall perimeter may not share the same wetting or freezing exposure. Ask the assessor to divide them on the plan and explain each termination. A system selected for a conditioned interior should not be assumed suitable beyond the door. Coordinate snow removal so blades, chains, and stored piles do not damage terminations or hold salty water against walls. Keep drains and collection points functional through the season. When spring cleaning reveals aggregate loss, hollow patches, widening cracks, or rust staining, pause cosmetic repair and obtain the appropriate concrete evaluation. Owners should also record which de-icing products are used on site or tracked in by vehicles when known. Product names and safety sheets give the assessor more useful information than calling every residue “salt.” Surface Preparation for a flake floor Primary references Sources and further reading Alberta Infrastructure: De-Icing Concrete Government of Alberta · Technical bulletin on de-icers, concrete durability, and spring washing. ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Concrete repair and protective-system selection guidance. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/services/concrete-solutions
Surface Preparation and Concrete Repair in Edmonton | Final Finish

Surface Preparation · Repair · Crack Filling Surface Preparation and concrete repair. The concrete decides what the floor can be. Grinding, repair, levelling and Crack Filling come before any colour, on every Final Finish floor. Final Finish · Edmonton What it is Three services, each for a different job. Surface Preparation Surface Preparation is the work that gets a concrete slab ready to hold a coating. The room is cleared, the condition of the floor is recorded, old coatings, oil and loose material come off, and the slab is diamond ground to open the surface. It is part of every Final Finish floor, and it decides how long the floor lasts. The grinding guide covers edges, dust, and what a scope should record. Concrete Repair, Levelling and Diamond Grinding Diamond grinding opens the slab with diamond tooling so a coating can bond, and takes off what is already there. Concrete repair fills and rebuilds spalls and damaged areas, and levelling brings a floor back toward flat where low spots or elevation changes make it hard to use or to coat evenly. Larger repairs are quoted as their own line, with their own material and sequence. The levelling guide explains flat versus level. Crack Filling Crack Filling is part of every coating job. After the grind, visible cracks are filled so they do not read through the finish. A crack that keeps opening is a movement question, not a filler question, and Denis says so before work starts.
